:::{#thm-gram-schmidt}
#### What Gram-Schmidt produces

Run the Gram-Schmidt process (@def-gram-schmidt) on $\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_k \in \reals^p$.

1. If it has produced $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_i$ without stopping,
   then $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_i$ are orthonormal
   and $\operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_i}
   = \operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_i}$.
2. If it reaches step $i$ (that is, it did not stop at steps $1, \ldots, i - 1$),
   it stops there
   exactly when $\vecf{a}_i \in \operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_{i-1}}$.
3. It completes all $k$ steps
   exactly when $\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_k$ are linearly independent;
   then $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_k$ is an orthonormal basis
   of $\operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_k}$ (@def-orthonormal-basis).

:::

::: proof

**Parts 1 and 2, by [induction](proof-writing.qmd#def-proof-by-induction) on $i$.**
Before step $1$, the list of $\vecf{q}$'s is empty,
which is orthonormal, and both spans are $\cb{\vzero}$ (@def-span).
Suppose part 1 holds after step $i - 1$,
and write $\mathcal{S}_{i-1} = \operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_{i-1}}
= \operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_{i-1}}$.
The orthonormal vectors $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_{i-1}$ are linearly independent
(@thm-orthonormal-independent) and span $\mathcal{S}_{i-1}$,
so they are an orthonormal basis of it.

*$\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i$ is orthogonal to the earlier $\vecf{q}$'s.*
For each $l < i$,

$$
\ba
\vecf{q}_l \cdot \tilde{\vecf{q}}_i
&= \vecf{q}_l \cdot \paren{1\,\vecf{a}_i + \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \paren{-\vecf{q}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i}\,\vecf{q}_j}
&& \text{(@def-gram-schmidt, as a linear combination)}
\\
&= 1\,(\vecf{q}_l \cdot \vecf{a}_i) + \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \paren{-\vecf{q}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i}\,(\vecf{q}_l \cdot \vecf{q}_j)
&& \text{(@thm-dot-linear-sum)}
\\
&= \vecf{q}_l \cdot \vecf{a}_i - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} (\vecf{q}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i)\,(\vecf{q}_l \cdot \vecf{q}_j)
&& \text{(} 1\,z = z \text{, and pull the minus signs out of the sum)}
\\
&= \vecf{q}_l \cdot \vecf{a}_i - \vecf{q}_l \cdot \vecf{a}_i
&& \text{(only the } j = l \text{ term survives, @def-orthonormal-vectors)}
\\
&= 0.
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\ea
$$

*Part 2 at step $i$.*
If $\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i = \vzero$, then
$\vecf{a}_i = \sum_{j<i} (\vecf{q}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i)\,\vecf{q}_j \in \mathcal{S}_{i-1}$.
Conversely, if $\vecf{a}_i \in \mathcal{S}_{i-1}$, then
$\vecf{a}_i = \sum_{j<i} (\vecf{q}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i)\,\vecf{q}_j$
(@thm-orthonormal-expansion), so $\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i = \vzero$.

*Part 1 at step $i$, if the process does not stop.*
Then $\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i \ne \vzero$, so $\norm{\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i} > 0$,
and $\vecf{q}_i = \tilde{\vecf{q}}_i / \norm{\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i}$ has
norm $\norm{\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i} / \norm{\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i} = 1$ (@thm-norm-properties)
and for $l < i$

$$
\ba
\vecf{q}_l \cdot \vecf{q}_i
&= \frac{1}{\norm{\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i}}\,(\vecf{q}_l \cdot \tilde{\vecf{q}}_i)
&& \text{(@thm-dot-linear, special case } b = 0 \text{)}
\\
&= 0,
&& \text{(} \tilde{\vecf{q}}_i \text{ is orthogonal to } \vecf{q}_l \text{)}
\ea
$$

and $\vecf{q}_i \cdot \vecf{q}_l = 0$ too (@thm-lincom-symmetric).
So $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_i$ are orthonormal.
For the spans:

- $\vecf{a}_i = \norm{\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i}\,\vecf{q}_i + \sum_{j<i} (\vecf{q}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i)\,\vecf{q}_j$
  is in $\operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_i}$,
  and so is each of $\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_{i-1}$, which lie in
  $\mathcal{S}_{i-1} = \operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_{i-1}}
  \subseteq \operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_i}$.
- $\vecf{q}_i = \paren{\vecf{a}_i - \sum_{j<i} (\vecf{q}_j \cdot \vecf{a}_i)\,\vecf{q}_j} / \norm{\tilde{\vecf{q}}_i}$
  is in $\operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_i}$,
  because each $\vecf{q}_j$ with $j < i$ lies in $\mathcal{S}_{i-1}$;
  and so is each of $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_{i-1}$.

A span is a subspace (@thm-span-subspace),
so it contains every linear combination of vectors in it;
each span therefore contains the other, and they are equal.

**Part 3.**
If the process completes, then $\vecf{a}_1 \notin \operatorname{span}$ of the empty list,
and for each $i \ge 2$, $\vecf{a}_i \notin \operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_{i-1}}$
(part 2).
Applying @thm-add-outside-span $k$ times, starting from the empty list,
shows that $\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_k$ are linearly independent.
Conversely, if they are linearly independent,
no $\vecf{a}_i$ is a linear combination $\sum_{j<i} c_j \vecf{a}_j$ of the earlier ones,
because then $\sum_{j<i} c_j \vecf{a}_j - \vecf{a}_i = \vzero$
would be a combination with a nonzero coefficient;
so by part 2 the process never stops.
When it completes, $\vecf{q}_1, \ldots, \vecf{q}_k$ are orthonormal, hence linearly independent
(@thm-orthonormal-independent),
and span $\operatorname{span}\cb{\vecf{a}_1, \ldots, \vecf{a}_k}$ (part 1),
so they are an orthonormal basis of it.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-thm-gram-schmidt}
#### Finishing an orthonormal basis of $\reals^3$

Continue @exm-gram-schmidt with $\vecf{a}_3 = (0, 1, 1)$.
$\vecf{q}_1 \cdot \vecf{a}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and
$\vecf{q}_2 \cdot \vecf{a}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\,(0 - 1 + 2) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$, so

$$
\ba
\tilde{\vecf{q}}_3
&= (0, 1, 1) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,(1, 1, 0) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \cd \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\,(1, -1, 2)
&& \text{(orthogonalize)}
\\
&= (0, 1, 1) - \tfrac{1}{2}\,(1, 1, 0) - \tfrac{1}{6}\,(1, -1, 2)
&& \text{(multiply the scalars)}
\\
&= \paren{0 - \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{6},\; 1 - \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{6},\; 1 - 0 - \tfrac{2}{6}}
&& \text{(subtract entrywise)}
\\
&= \paren{-\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}},
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\ea
$$

with norm $\sqrt{3 \cd \tfrac{4}{9}} = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$,
so $\vecf{q}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,(-1, 1, 1)$.
The process did not stop,
so by @thm-gram-schmidt
$\vecf{a}_1, \vecf{a}_2, \vecf{a}_3$ are linearly independent
and $\vecf{q}_1, \vecf{q}_2, \vecf{q}_3$ is an orthonormal basis of their span.
That span therefore has dimension $3$ (@def-dimension),
so it is $\reals^3$ (@thm-subspace-equal-dim, @exm-dimension).
As a check,
$\vecf{q}_1 \cdot \vecf{q}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\,(-1 + 1 + 0) = 0$
and $\vecf{q}_2 \cdot \vecf{q}_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{18}}\,(-1 - 1 + 2) = 0$.

:::
